title: Ask about a selection
Options
text:
Ask about a selection — Options
| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `quote.fromAnswer` | `true` | Selecting text inside an answer offers *Ask AI* on it. |
| `quote.fromDocs` | `false` | Selecting text in the article offers *Ask AI* too. Navigation, sidebar and footer are never quotable. |
| `ui.firstRunHint` | `false` | Shows a one-time line in the empty panel: *Select any passage to ask about it.* |

The quote is sent with the question and stays visible in the question bubble, so the thread shows what was asked about. A quoted selection is scrubbed for keys the same way the question is — see Pasted keys (/features/credentials).

The article is found with `host.article` — `.vp-doc, main` on VitePress. On another site, set it to the element that holds your content.

More: `quote` (/reference/config#quote) in the reference.

title: Static or server
How to choose
text:
Static or server — How to choose
Ask three questions. One "yes" is enough for the server install.

| question | if yes |
|---|---|
| Must the corpus, the prompt or the thresholds stay off the page? | server |
| Do you need rate limits, a daily cap or metrics without writing proxy rules? | server |
| Do you want a turn log to feed `traffic` and `dataset`? | server |

Three "no" answers mean the static install: public pages, nothing extra to run and keep. `npx docpilot init` asks the same thing as *Where should a question be answered?* and prints the block to paste for either answer.

title: What changes between them
text:
Static or server — What changes between them
| | static | server |
|---|---|---|
| the turn runs in | the reader's browser | `@cloflin/docpilot/server` |
| the page downloads | the index, the prompt, the thresholds | the page list, cited passages, the stream |
| you run | nothing new — the `/ai` proxy forwards model calls | `npx docpilot serve` or `createDocPilotServer` |
| limits and metrics | yours, in the proxy | built in, on by default |
| follow-up chips | yes | no |

The server install keeps the index from being downloaded in bulk. It does not make the content secret: a reader can still read every passage an answer cites.

title: Change later
text:
Static or server — Change later
Both installs read the same index, built by the same `npx docpilot index`, so the switch is one setting. Score the same golden set through each before you switch:

```bash
npx docpilot eval --runtime=browser --quiet
npx docpilot eval --runtime=server --quiet
```

Moving to the server install also means: stop publishing the index, put the server behind the proxy that serves the site, and set `DOCPILOT_SERVER_SECRET` and `DOCPILOT_METRICS_TOKEN`.

More: Choose your install (/install/choose) for the full comparison, The server runtime (/guide/server) to set it up, and Server operations (/guide/server-operations) for limits and metrics.

title: Search scope
Options
text:
Search scope — Options
| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `scope.enabled` | `true` | Shows the chip and the picker. `false` always searches everything. |
| `scope.groupBySection` | `true` | Groups the page list under your sidebar headings. Flat while the reader is filtering. |
| `scope.filter` | `'auto'` | Adds a filter field above the list when there are more than `promptListLimit` pages. |
| `scope.promptListLimit` | `12` | How many pages the list shows before the filter appears. |
| `suggestions.scoped` | `true` | Under a narrow scope, the empty panel lists the scoped pages instead of generic suggestions. |

When the scope is too narrow
If the answer is not inside the chosen pages, the panel does not quietly widen the search. It says *I couldn't find this in this page*, lists the **closest pages elsewhere**, and offers one button: *Clear the scope and search all docs*.

A link can set the scope too: `?dp-ask=…&dp-scope=page` — see Deep links (/features/triggers#deep-links).

More: `scope` (/reference/config#scope) in the reference.

title: Panel shapes
1. Bar
text:
Panel shapes — 1. Bar
The question box is on every page, at the bottom centre. The reader starts typing, the bar widens, and a window with the conversation rises above it. The field stays in the bar; the window holds everything else — the header, the thread, the scope, the footnote.

```ts
ui: { panel: 'bar' }
```

The bar takes the place of the floating button, and `ui.side` does not apply to it, because it is centred. Esc, the close button or a press elsewhere on the page closes the window; the bar stays, with a button that brings the conversation back. With the floating button in the trigger list and `panel` left at `'auto'`, this is the shape the panel opens in.

2. Popup
A floating button in the corner, and the conversation in a popup above it. The popup covers a corner of the page and nothing else; the button turns into a chevron while it is open.

```ts
ui: { trigger: 'fab', panel: 'popup' }
```

`ui.side` moves the button and the popup together — `'left'` puts both in the bottom-left corner. `ui.fabLabel` sets the words on the button, or `false` for the icon alone.

title: 3. Push panel
text:
Panel shapes — 3. Push panel
A drawer the full height of the window, docked to an edge. With `layout: 'push'` the page narrows beside it instead of being covered, and moves back as the drawer leaves.

```ts
ui: { panel: 'drawer', layout: 'push', side: 'end' }    // the trailing edge
ui: { panel: 'drawer', layout: 'push', side: 'left' }   // a sidebar on the left
```

What moves is the host adapter's decision: on VitePress the whole layout narrows and the article re-centres; on Docusaurus `.main-wrapper` is padded. Any other host gets classes on `` — `docpilot-push`, `docpilot-push-start`, `docpilot-push-end` — and styles its own wrapper from them. Without `layout: 'push'`, the drawer covers that side of the page.

title: On a phone
text:
Panel shapes — On a phone
Below 960 px all three shapes are the same full-screen sheet. The bar becomes a button at the bottom centre that opens it, and `layout: 'push'` does nothing, because there is no page beside the sheet to move.

More: `ui.panel` (/reference/config#ui-panel), `ui.layout` (/reference/config#ui-layout) and `ui.side` (/reference/config#ui-side) in the reference, Triggers and layout (/features/triggers) for the doors into the panel, and Appearance (/guide/appearance) for the tokens that size each shape.

title: Skills for your agent
text:
Skills for your agent — Skills for your agent
npx docpilot init copies the DocPilot skills, the /docpilot-* slash commands and the tuning agents into your agent tool; the agent reads them and runs the CLI; npx docpilot update refreshes them and keeps your edits.
DocPilot ships the written half of running it as Agent Skills: what to measure, what has already been measured, and what an edit may not break. `npx docpilot init` copies them into the agent tool you name, so Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Copilot can run the CLI by the same rules you would. The mock-up plays the three acts: copy, use, refresh.

```bash
npx docpilot init --target=claude --scope=project   # copy skills, commands, agents
npx docpilot update --dry                            # what an upgrade would change
npx docpilot update                                  # refresh, keep your edits as .bak
```

title: 1. `init` copies them
text:
Skills for your agent — 1. `init` copies them
A skill inside `node_modules` reaches nobody: every agent tool looks for skills in the project or in your home directory, never in a dependency. So `init` copies them, and asks where:

| question | flag | answers |
|---|---|---|
| Which agent tool? | `--target=` | `claude`, `codex`, `cursor`, `copilot`, `agents` — a comma list works |
| This project, or you on this machine? | `--scope=` | `project` (committed with the repo) or `user` (your home directory) |

Into that tool's directory go three skills, one slash command per CLI command, and — for Claude Code only — two subagents:

| what | for |
|---|---|
| `docs-rag` | the measurement and tuning loop: eval, golden sets, the bench, openers, and the list of things already measured |
| `docs-import` | the contract for pages imported from another site |
| `docs-tune` | the improvement loop the tuning agents follow |
| `/docpilot-index`, `/docpilot-eval`, … | each command with its own flags, generated from the table the CLI validates against |
| `docpilot-tuner`, `docpilot-writer` | the Claude Code agents (/guide/tuning-agent) that run the loop and write one edit at a time |

title: 2. The agent reads them
text:
Skills for your agent — 2. The agent reads them
Ask for a measurement — `/docpilot-eval`, or "why does the panel miss this question?" — and the agent reads `docs-rag` first. The skill tells it which command to run, how to read the report, and which experiments not to repeat. The binding rules hold whoever is reading: the thresholds are not levers, an LLM judge never gates, and a change that regresses a metric by more than two points is reverted.

The copies are yours. Edit them: the numbers inside are about the corpus this package was developed against, not yours.

title: 3. `update` refreshes them
text:
Skills for your agent — 3. `update` refreshes them
`init` never overwrites, which makes it safe to re-run and useless for an upgrade. After `npm install @cloflin/docpilot@latest`, run `npx docpilot update`. Beside every skill sits `.docpilot.json` with a hash per file, so:

- a file nobody touched is replaced in silence;
- a file **you edited** is replaced, and your copy is kept beside it as `.bak`, named in the report.

With no flags, `update` finds every install on the machine. `--check` fails a CI job when the copies are behind the package.

More: Skills (/reference/skills) for what each skill contains, `init` (/reference/cli#init) and `update` (/reference/cli#update) in the CLI reference, and Tune with Claude Code (/guide/tuning-agent) for the agents.

title: Sources and passages
Options
text:
Sources and passages — Options
| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `citations.passage` | `false` | Adds *Show the passage* to each source row. The text comes from the turn itself, so opening it costs nothing. |
| `citations.inCopy` | `true` | *Copy answer* appends a `Sources:` heading with absolute Markdown links, so a pasted answer still points home. |
| `citations.pagesRead` | `false` | When the panel cannot answer, it lists the pages it searched under *Searched the docs and read 4 pages*. |

title: What is checked
text:
Sources and passages — What is checked
The sources are not whatever the model claims. Before an answer is shown, the browser compares every citation with the passages it actually retrieved for that turn:

- A citation to a passage that was not retrieved is removed.
- A citation of one of the site's own tools (/features/tools) passes the same check, because the browser handed out its id that turn. It shows as *Plan limits · from the site*, with no link and no passage.
- A link to a page that does not exist on your site is shown as text, not as a link.
- If the model marks itself unsure, the answer says so: *The model was unsure of this one — check the sources below.*

On a restored conversation, the passage is looked up again by its id. If a rebuild removed it, the row has no chevron instead of a stale passage.

More: `citations` (/reference/config#citations) in the reference, and What it guarantees (/concepts/guarantees).

title: Status and reasoning
text:
Status and reasoning — Status and reasoning
The reader sees what the assistant is doing — loading, searching, reading a page, thinking, writing — and how long a reasoning model thought.
A wait without information feels broken. While a turn runs, one line under the question names the current step, and a reasoning model's thinking sits in a collapsible block that opens while it thinks and closes when the answer starts.

```ts
docPilot: {
  chat: { reasoning: 'auto' },      // or 'low' | 'medium' | 'high' | false
  ui: { waitingEscalation: true },  // "Still working" after 8 s
}
```

title: The steps
text:
Status and reasoning — The steps
| Line | When |
|---|---|
| *Loading the docs index* | the first question, while the index downloads |
| *Searching the docs* | retrieval in the browser |
| *Looking at the page list* | the model asked for the list of pages |
| *Reading guide/webhooks* | the model opened a section |
| *Checking Plan limits* | one of the site's own tools (/features/tools) is running; the line names its `title` |
| *Thinking* | a reasoning model before its first word |
| *Writing the answer* | the answer is streaming |

With `ui.waitingEscalation`, a turn with no answer yet says *Still working* at 8 seconds, and *Still working — the answer has not started yet* at 25. After a reasoning model finishes, the block reads *Thought for 4s* and stays available to open.

Options
| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `chat.reasoning` | `'auto'` | Asks a reasoning model to think, and shows the thinking. `false` turns it off; a level or `{ effort, budgetTokens, visible }` tunes it. |
| `ui.waitingEscalation` | `true` | The *Still working* lines. |

More: `chat.reasoning` (/reference/config#chat-reasoning) in the reference.

title: Suggestions
Options
text:
Suggestions — Options
| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `suggestions.questions` | `[]` | Your starter questions. With none, three generic ones are shown. A plain array of strings works too. |
| `suggestions.precomputed` | `true` | `npx docpilot index` runs retrieval for each question at build time, so a click needs no embedding call. |
| `suggestions.answers` | `true` | Also writes the answer at build time, so a click costs no request at all. Served only in the language it was written in. |
| `suggestions.authored` | `[]` | Answers you write yourself, `{ q, answer, cite }`, served verbatim. |
| `suggestions.reveal` | `true` | Paints a prepared answer in over about 1.4 seconds instead of all at once. |
| `suggestions.scoped` | `true` | Under a narrow scope, the rows become the pages in scope. |
| `suggestions.followUps` | `false` | Adds *Follow-up questions* under the newest answer. |
| `suggestions.matchTau` / `matchCos` | `0.65` / `0.72` | How close a typed question must be to a prepared one to reuse its answer. |

`product` names your product in the placeholder (*Ask about Acme*) and in the greeting. A *hello*, *thanks* or *who are you* is answered from a template in the reader's language, with no model call — see Social openers (/guide/social-openers).

More: `suggestions` (/reference/config#suggestions) in the reference.

title: The terminal
text:
The terminal — The terminal
The DocPilot command line shows the numbers — a home screen with a menu of next steps, docpilot status for the state of a project, docpilot monitor for a live server, progress bars, an eval scorecard, and colour rules that never break a log.
Run `npx docpilot` in a terminal and it shows where your project stands and what to do next. Three parts make that up: the **home screen**, `docpilot status` and `docpilot monitor`. The progress bars and the eval scorecard that the other commands draw follow the same rules. The mock-up plays a first session on an imaginary site: `init`, `index`, `eval --gate-only`, then `status` naming the next step.

```bash
npx docpilot init               # the skills, the install, where the panel goes
npx docpilot index              # build the index
npx docpilot eval --gate-only   # measure retrieval; no model is called
npx docpilot status             # where the project stands, and what to run next
```

This page is about what you see and when. Every flag is in the CLI reference (/reference/cli).

**Availability.** The home screen, `status`, the progress bars and the scorecard work with both installs. `monitor` reads a running server, so it needs the server install (/install/choose). All of it is new in 2.0, and none of it changes what a reader sees.

title: The home screen
text:
The terminal — The home screen
```bash
npx docpilot
```

On a terminal it prints the picture of the project that `status` prints, then a menu of the commands that make sense now. The first entry is the project's next step, so Enter runs it.

| key | does |
|---|---|
| ↑ and ↓, or `k` and `j` | Move |
| a digit | Pick that entry |
| Enter | Run the selected command |
| Esc or `q` | Back out |
| Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D | Exit with code `130` |

Each entry runs the real command in your terminal, with its own questions and its own exit code.

**The menu appears only when stdin and stdout are both a terminal and `CI` is not set.** Anything else — a pipe, a CI job, `--help` — prints the help exactly as 1.x did. A script that ran `npx docpilot` before still gets the same text. See the home screen (/reference/cli#home-screen).

title: docpilot status
text:
The terminal — docpilot status
```bash
npx docpilot status
npx docpilot status --json
```

`status` is one picture of the project and the one command to run next. It reads files on disk and talks to no network unless you pass `--url` or the project runs `runtime: 'server'`.

| block | tells you |
|---|---|
| project | The runtime, the config path, where the docs, the index and the eval sets live |
| index | Fresh or stale, the hash, chunks and pages, the embedder, and the size on disk and over brotli |
| guard | `guard.mode`, the thresholds the index ships and where they came from |
| eval sets | Counts of golden records by `expect`, `split` and `level`, and of the other sets |
| last eval | The newest report as a scorecard: each metric, its move since the last comparable run, and a sparkline |
| server | Whether the server answers, the round trip, the index it serves and its metrics |
| next | The command to run, and why |

**Fresh means the hash the build would write.** `status` chunks the docs again, offline, and compares the hash with the manifest's. A site with imported pages, OpenAPI specs or a built-HTML source is reported *unverified*, not stale, because `status` cannot re-read those sources.

**It always exits `0` when it ran.** A stale index is a finding, not a failure. `doctor` (/reference/cli#doctor) is the command a CI job exits on.

`--json` prints one object, `{"kind": "docpilot.status", "v": 1, …}`, and nothing else. `next.rule` names the rule that chose the next step, so a script or an agent branches on a name and not on a sentence. The rules, and the keys of the object, are in the `status` reference (/reference/cli#status).

title: docpilot monitor
text:
The terminal — docpilot monitor
```bash
npx docpilot monitor --url=https://docs.example.com/ai/turn --token=$DOCPILOT_METRICS_TOKEN
```

`monitor` polls a running server's `GET {endpoint}/metrics?format=json` and redraws one block in place: turns per minute with a sparkline of the last thirty minutes, latency percentiles, first-token time, the time each stage took, a bar for each outcome, errors and rate-limited turns, tokens, and the model and index the server runs. `q` quits.

- **Off a terminal it prints one JSON line per poll**, so the same command feeds a log: `npx docpilot monitor --interval=10s >> metrics.jsonl`.
- **`--once`** polls one time, prints the snapshot as a JSON line and exits `0`, or `1` with the reason on stderr.
- **A field that is missing is drawn as `—`.** A server that has answered no turn has no p95.
- **A server without a metrics route** answers `404` and `monitor` says *metrics unavailable* instead of failing. A server that wants a token answers `401`, and off loopback with no token `403`. For both, `monitor` names the variable to set.

What the numbers mean, and the setting that turns the route off, are in Server operations (/guide/server-operations#metrics). The flags are in the `monitor` reference (/reference/cli#monitor).

title: Progress and the scorecard
text:
The terminal — Progress and the scorecard
Long commands show where they are.

- `index`, `eval`, `calibrate` and `tune` draw a progress bar with an ETA.
- `eval` ends with a **scorecard**: each metric, its move since the run `eval` compared it with, and a sparkline across earlier comparable runs. A metric that moved the good way is green, whichever way that is: up for recall, down for latency.
- A warning that repeats prints once, followed by `×N`, so a log shows what happened and how often and not three hundred lines of it.

Measure (/guide/measure) explains the metrics in the scorecard.

title: Colour
text:
The terminal — Colour
Colour carries meaning — green for good, yellow for a warning, red for a failure — and never carries a fact alone. The words are the same with the colour off.

A stream is coloured when all of these hold, checked in this order:

1. `NO_COLOR` is not set to a non-empty value. If it is, there is no colour, whatever else is set.
2. `FORCE_COLOR` is not set. If it is set to an empty string, `1`, `2`, `3` or `true`, colour is on, even through a pipe. Any other value, `0` and `false` included, turns it off.
3. Otherwise, the stream is a terminal and `TERM` is not `dumb`.

So piped output has no colour escape codes and is the 1.x output, and a CI log stays readable. Set `FORCE_COLOR=1` to keep colour through a pager or a CI log that renders it.

Related
- CLI reference (/reference/cli) — every command and flag.
- Server operations (/guide/server-operations) — the metrics `monitor` reads.
- Improve answers (/guide/improving) — the loop that `status` points to once a site is measured.

title: Tools and actions
Two kinds
text:
Tools and actions — Two kinds
`confirm` decides which one a tool is.

| `confirm` | kind | who runs it | what the reader sees |
|---|---|---|---|
| `false` (default) | **function tool** | the model calls it while it searches, and DocPilot runs it at once | "Checking Plan limits", then a source row **from the site** under the answer |
| `true` | **action** | the reader, with one press | a button under the answer, with your `label` |
| `'form'` | **action** | the reader, after reviewing the arguments | a button that opens a form with the model's suggestions filled in |

A function tool must only *read*. The build stops on a function tool that would `POST`, navigate or fire an event, because none of those can answer the model and each of them changes something without the reader. Make it an action instead.

title: A function tool
text:
Tools and actions — A function tool
```ts
plan_limits: {
  description: 'Live limits of one plan: requests per day, seats and storage.',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: { plan: { type: 'string', enum: ['free', 'pro', 'team'] } },
    required: ['plan'],
  },
  run: { fetch: '/api/plans/{plan}' },
}
```

On a question that needs it:

1. The model calls `plan_limits({plan: 'pro'})` on a search step, next to the built-in `search_docs`.
2. DocPilot checks the arguments against your schema. A call that fails the check never runs, and the model is told why.
3. The tool runs, with a 10-second limit: here, a `GET` to `/api/plans/pro`.
4. The model receives the reply as data, with an id it can cite. The model sees up to 4,000 characters of it.
5. The answer cites the reply like a page, and the source row reads **Plan limits · from the site**. A cited answer stays on screen. An answer with no citation is withdrawn, as before.

The same call with the same arguments a second time in a turn is answered from the first and costs nothing.

title: An action
text:
Tools and actions — An action
```ts
open_pricing: {
  description: 'Open the pricing page for one plan.',
  label: 'Open pricing',
  parameters: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: { plan: { type: 'string', enum: ['free', 'pro', 'team'] } },
    required: ['plan'],
  },
  confirm: true,
  run: { href: '/pricing?plan={plan}' },
}
```

The model never runs an action. It may offer up to three with its answer, each with arguments it took from the conversation, and the reader decides:

- **A button** (`confirm: true`) shows your `label`, and on a second line the model's arguments, such as "With plan: pro", because "Open pricing" for the wrong plan is a different action. The arguments are part of the button's name, so a screen reader reads them too.
- **A form** (`confirm: 'form'`) opens under the answer. It has one field per parameter, labelled with the parameter's `description`, and the model's suggestions are filled in. The reader can change any value. DocPilot checks what the reader sends against your schema before anything is sent.
- **The outcome** appears where the button was. It is your endpoint's own words when the reply is a string or has a `message` field, and **Done.** otherwise. If the action fails, the button comes back so the reader can try again.

The model offers an action only when it is the obvious next step for the question, or when the reader asked for it. A document or a tool result that tells the model to offer one is ignored. A restored conversation shows its answers without their actions, so yesterday's "Contact support" cannot be sent twice by accident.

title: What runs a tool
What runs a tool
text:
Tools and actions — What runs a tool
`registerTool` is exported from `@cloflin/docpilot/theme`, `/vue`, `/react`, `/mount` and `/web`. A ``-tag install has it as `window.DocPilot.registerTool`. It returns a function that removes the handler again. A handler receives the checked arguments and `{question, page, signal}`, and whatever it returns is the tool's result.

A function `run` cannot reach a static page, because `themeConfig` is JSON. The build stops on one, and the message names `registerTool` instead.

title: Writing a tool the model uses well
text:
Tools and actions — Writing a tool the model uses well
The model chooses a tool by its `description` and fills it by its `parameters`. The rules that make it choose well are the ones OpenAI and Anthropic publish for function calling:

- **Say when to use it, and when not to.** "Live limits of one plan. Use it for a question about current limits; the pricing page covers what each plan includes." A description that says only "Gets plan limits" leaves the model to guess when it applies.
- **Use `enum` for every closed set.** `plan: {enum: ['free', 'pro', 'team']}` cannot be called with `'premium'`.
- **Do not ask for what your code already knows.** The page and the question reach your handler, and a same-origin `fetch` carries the reader's cookies. A parameter for any of them is a value the model can get wrong.
- **One tool per question it answers.** If two tools are always called one after the other, make them one.
- **Keep the set small.** Twelve is the ceiling. A handful the model can tell apart works better than twelve it confuses.
- **Return what the answer needs.** The reply goes to the model and to your model provider. A short JSON object with the numbers the answer will quote is better than a whole account record.

title: Parameters
text:
Tools and actions — Parameters
`parameters` is a flat JSON Schema object. Each property is a `string`, `number`, `integer` or `boolean`, with these optional keys:

| key | for | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `description` | every type | tells the model what the value is, and labels the form field |
| `enum` | every type | the allowed values; a form shows them as buttons |
| `default` | every type | the value an empty field takes; the model is told it, and a form starts from it. The build refuses a default that the parameter itself would refuse |
| `format` | `string` | `email`, `uri` or `date` set the input type; `multiline` asks for a text area |
| `maxLength` | `string` | the longest allowed value |
| `minimum`, `maximum` | `number`, `integer` | the allowed range |

`required` lists the values a call must have. A form action is the one exception: the reader can supply a missing required value in the form. DocPilot sends the model a strict version of the schema, in which every property is required and an optional one may be `null`. DocPilot enforces `enum`, `format` and the bounds in code, because providers disagree on which of those keywords a strict schema may carry. Nested objects and arrays are not supported yet.

title: On a server install
text:
Tools and actions — On a server install
| | static install | server install |
|---|---|---|
| function tools | run in the reader's browser: a registered handler, or a `fetch` that resolves on your page and carries its cookies | run on your server: a function `run`, or a `fetch` to an absolute URL |
| actions | run in the browser | proposed by the server, run in the browser |

The page receives only the actions, without their descriptions, because the descriptions are written for the model. The server's turn log records each function call as `{tool, ok, ms}`, never its arguments or its reply. The server's default turn is one-shot and has no search step, so a function tool needs `server.turn.loop: 'agentic'` there.

title: What it costs
text:
Tools and actions — What it costs
- A function call is one search step. It is charged like a search and capped by `maxIterations` (/reference/config#maxiterations). A turn that runs one-shot, which is the default on a server and on a nearly spent free tier, offers no function tools.
- Actions ride on the answer call and cost no extra request in either mode.
- Models without native tool calling get the tools as text, in the same protocol as the built-in ones. gpt-6-luna takes function tools only with reasoning off, and DocPilot sends that on search steps by itself.

title: Not yet
text:
Tools and actions — Not yet
- **An approval in the middle of a search.** Every write is an action at the end of an answer. A turn does not pause for the reader and then continue.
- **Nested parameters.** A parameter is a string, a number, an integer or a boolean.
- **Reasoning together with tools on GPT-6.** That needs the Responses API, which DocPilot does not use yet. Search steps run with reasoning off.
- **Measuring your tools.** `docpilot eval` runs its probes without them.
- **Keeping actions.** A restored conversation shows its answers and sources, not their actions.

title: Safety
text:
Tools and actions — Safety
- **Nothing that changes anything runs without the reader.** A function tool can only read, and an action needs a press or a sent form.
- **Every word on a button is yours.** The model chooses which action to offer and with which values. The text on the button is your `label`.
- **The arguments are checked in code** against your schema, and they are URL-encoded into a template. The build refuses a placeholder in the scheme or the host, and an argument that makes a `.` or `..` segment fails the call, so the model controls neither the host nor the path.
- **A tool's reply is data, not instruction.** It reaches the model under the same rule as a documentation section, cut to 4,000 characters.
- **A page that tries to steer the model can at most propose a button.** DocPilot's own security bench (/guide/benchmarks) measured 23–30 % success for planted instructions. That is why a model never decides alone what runs.

The design and its research are in engine-spec 038 (https://github.com/Cloflin/docpilot/blob/main/engine-specs/038-tools-the-site-adds.md) and ui-spec 018 (https://github.com/Cloflin/docpilot/blob/main/ui-specs/018-actions-the-answer-offers.md). Every key is in the configuration reference (/reference/config#tools).

title: Triggers and layout
Options
text:
Triggers and layout — Options
| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ui.trigger` | `'fab'` | Where the buttons go. `'nav'` puts an icon beside search and a row in the mobile menu; `'fab'` a floating button; `'both'` all three; `'none'` no button. |
| `ui.panel` | `'auto'` | `'popup'` floats above the button; `'drawer'` takes the full height at the edge; `'bar'` puts a question bar at the bottom centre and raises the conversation above it as the reader types, in place of the floating button. `'auto'` picks the bar when the floating placement is in the list, the drawer when it is not, and never the popup. |
| `ui.side` | `'end'` | The edge the floating button, its popup and the drawer sit at: `'left'`, `'right'`, or `'start'`/`'end'` to follow the page's text direction. |
| `ui.fabLabel` | `true` | The words on the corner button under `'popup'` or `'drawer'`: `true` shows *Ask AI*, a string shows that text, `false` shows the icon alone. |
| `ui.layout` | `'overlay'` | `'push'` narrows the page instead of covering it when the drawer opens, from whichever edge `ui.side` names. |
| `ui.background` | `'notify'` | An answer that finishes while the panel is closed puts a dot on the trigger; `'open'` reopens the panel instead. |
| `ui.prefetch` | `'hover'` | Starts fetching the index when the pointer reaches a trigger, so the first answer starts sooner. |

Below 960 px the panel is a full-screen sheet, whatever the setting. ⌘ I works on every page, even with `trigger: 'none'`; Esc closes the panel, or stops an answer that is still being written.

Deep links
`composer.deepLink` (on by default) lets a link open the panel with a question already typed:

```
https://docs.example.com/guide/webhooks?dp-ask=How+do+retries+work&dp-scope=page
```

title: Options
text:
Triggers and layout — Options
The question is filled in, never sent. `dp-scope=page` narrows the search to the page the link lands on.

More: `ui` (/reference/config#ui) in the reference, and The assistant panel (/guide/panel).

title: Appearance
text:
Appearance — Appearance
The panel ships as one stylesheet that knows nothing about any host, plus one
small adapter per host that translates it into that host's own tokens. Everything
on this page follows from that split — which file to import, which custom
properties to override, and what the two placements actually do.

title: Five entry points
text:
Appearance — Five entry points
| import | what it is | when |
|---|---|---|
| `@cloflin/docpilot/style.css` | core + VitePress adapter | the default, and what `…/theme` already imports |
| `@cloflin/docpilot/style/core.css` | the panel, on real values | any other host, or your own mapping |
| `@cloflin/docpilot/style/vitepress.css` | the VitePress mapping only | you replaced the core and kept the host |
| `@cloflin/docpilot/style/docusaurus.css` | the Docusaurus mapping only | loaded for you by the Docusaurus plugin |
| `@cloflin/docpilot/web.css` | the core, from the prebuilt bundle | a `` tag, or the React adapter |

**All five are in `@layer docpilot`.** An unlayered rule beats a layered one
whatever its specificity, so any CSS your site already has wins over the panel's
without `!important` and without counting selectors — `.docpilot__send {
border-radius: 4px }` is enough. The core and an adapter share the one layer, so
the order below still decides between them.

**It points the other way too.** A reset your page loads unlayered outranks the
panel just as easily:

| host | what overrules the panel | what to do |
|---|---|---|
| VitePress 2 | nothing — its reset is in `@layer __vitepress_base`, and `style.css` names that layer before `docpilot` | — |
| VitePress 1 | the unlayered `base.css`: `button { padding: 0; background: transparent }`, `ul { list-style: none }`, `a { color: inherit }` | upgrade to VitePress 2 — there is no unlayered build to fall back on |
| Docusaurus | Infima's bare `h1`–`h6`, `ul`, `code`, `pre` and `a` in the answer body | turn on `future.v4.useCssCascadeLayers`, which puts Infima in a layer |
| Tailwind v3 | preflight's unlayered `* { border: 0 solid }` erases every hairline | Tailwind v4 layers it; on v3, declare the border back |

title: Five entry points
text:
Appearance — Five entry points
On a site whose own CSS is layered, the layer named first loses. Load the panel's
stylesheet after yours, or name the order yourself before anything else —
`@layer base, docpilot;` — and on VitePress 2 keep `__vitepress_base` ahead of
`docpilot` in that list.

**Three rules in the VitePress adapter stay outside the layer**, because each
exists to beat a declaration VitePress makes on its own component: the search
box's `flex-grow`, which would otherwise push the navbar trigger 398px away from
it, and the sidebar's `transition` in both directions of `ui.layout: 'push'`.
The still variant of that transition stays out with them, because it has to
cancel it.

An adapter is loaded **after** the core, always. The Docusaurus plugin lists them
in that order itself; everywhere else it is the order of your two imports.

`import { withDocPilot } from '@cloflin/docpilot/theme'` pulls in the bundle. To supply the CSS yourself:

```js
// docs/.vitepress/theme/index.js
import DefaultTheme from 'vitepress/theme'
import { withDocPilot } from '@cloflin/docpilot/theme-without-styles'
import '@cloflin/docpilot/style/core.css'
import './my-docpilot-tokens.css'

export default withDocPilot(DefaultTheme)
```

**Order is the mechanism, not a convention.** Inside `@layer docpilot` the core declares every token with a real value; the adapter re-declares the colour set on `:root` at the same specificity and wins by coming second. Load the adapter first and it loses. Your own tokens are outside the layer and win in any position. Load it alone and the panel has no styles at all — it declares no rules of its own, only a translation table.

title: Surfaces come in three levels
text:
Appearance — Surfaces come in three levels
This is the one thing worth knowing before the table. Everything the panel paints sits on one of three levels, and the level is what decides which token it uses:

| level | token | what wears it |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `--dp-surface` | the panel, and anything that **is** a surface — the composer, the code copy button, the floating button |
| 1 | `--dp-surface-2` | an **object's** own paint — the question bubble, a suggestion row, a pressed toggle's track, inline code — and a **row's** hover |
| 2 | `--dp-wash` | a pointer on a **control** — an icon button, a pill, an inline text button — composited *on top of* whatever it sits on |

A delete button inside a hovered history row therefore paints level 2 over level 1 and reads as a darker chip inside a lighter row. It separates by compositing, with no rule written for the case.

title: The tokens
text:
Appearance — The tokens
Everything the panel paints goes through one of these. The second column is what the core declares with no host; the two after it are what each adapter re-declares it as.

title: The tokens
text:
Appearance — The tokens

| token | core (light / dark) | on VitePress | on Docusaurus |

title: The tokens
text:
Appearance — The tokens
`--dp-wash` and `--dp-lip` are **derived rather than mapped**, and deliberately: substitution resolves it against whatever `--dp-text` ends up being, so it follows the host's theme — and your override of it — without a second declaration. Neither has a dark variant and neither may be given one; the suite requires every token that darkens to be re-declared unconditionally by an adapter, and no host token expresses "7% in light, 15% in dark" as one value.

`--dp-lip` is the **second and last border colour** in the package, and it is a different job from the hairline rather than a second one of it. The jump pill is glass over the thread — a translucent fill under `backdrop-filter: blur(2px)` — and a translucent thing with no light on its underside reads as a hole in the thread instead of an object over it. `--dp-line` still draws the pill's other three sides. Because it resolves against `--dp-text`, it is a near-white rim in dark and a grounded dark edge in light; a literal `rgba(255,255,255,.15)` would have been right in one scheme and invisible in the other.

title: The tokens
text:
Appearance — The tokens
`--dp-lip` is the **second and last border colour** in the package, and it is a different job from the hairline rather than a second one of it. The jump pill is glass over the thread — a translucent fill under `backdrop-filter: blur(2px)` — and a translucent thing with no light on its underside reads as a hole in the thread instead of an object over it. `--dp-line` still draws the pill's other three sides. Because it resolves against `--dp-text`, it is a near-white rim in dark and a grounded dark edge in light; a literal `rgba(255,255,255,.15)` would have been right in one scheme and invisible in the other.

`--dp-alert` is the **one colour in the package that is not part of your theme**, and the reason it is not mapped is the same reason it exists. It paints a single 10px dot on the trigger, and only when an answer settled while the panel was closed — see `ui.background` (/reference/config#ui-background). "There is something waiting" is not a statement any brand palette has a value for, so an adapter that reached for the host's own warning colour would be answering a question the host never asked; a site that disagrees repoints the one token. It has no dark variant because it needs none: the shipped literal clears the 3:1 non-text floor against both surfaces, at 4.8:1 on the light one and 3.6:1 on the dark. It is never text, never a border, and the only place it appears outside that dot is `forced-colors`, where the system palette takes it over entirely.

Geometry is declared once and does not vary with appearance:

title: The tokens
text:
Appearance — The tokens
Geometry is declared once and does not vary with appearance:

| token | value | for |
|---|---|---|
| `--dp-width` | `clamp(360px, 30vw, 460px)` | the drawer and the popup, deliberately the same |
| `--dp-bar-inline`, `--dp-bar-inline-open` | `400px`, `640px` | the bar under `panel: 'bar'` (/reference/config#ui-panel) at rest, and in use — focused, holding a question, or under its window, which takes the same width |
| `--dp-gutter` | `20px` | the panel's inline padding |
| `--dp-r-sm` | `8px` | icon buttons, the copy chip, the nav trigger, inline text buttons, inline code |
| `--dp-r-md` | `12px` | rows and blocks: suggestion, source, pick, the code card |
| `--dp-r-lg` | `16px` | the popup, the feedback textarea |
| `--dp-r-bubble` | `22px` | the question |
| `--dp-r-field` | `28px` | the composer |
| `--dp-r-pill` | `999px` | send, pills, the floating button, the status dot |
| `--dp-dur` | `400ms` | every entrance; every exit takes half of it |
| `--dp-dur-fast` | `150ms` | every colour, background and opacity change |
| `--dp-ease` | a spring as `linear()` — stiffness 350, damping 35, no visible overshoot | panels, the sheet, the pushed page, every press |
| `--dp-ease-pop` | a spring as `linear()` — stiffness 300, damping 25, a 3.8% overshoot | what pops: the popup, the bar and its window, a new question, a check glyph |
| `--dp-ease-exit` | `cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1)` | every exit — a thing that leaves accelerates away |
| `--dp-z` | `29`, `70` below 960px | above VitePress's own sidebar on the sheet |
| `--dp-fab-size`, `--dp-fab-size-coarse` | `48px`, `56px` | the floating button's **block** size |
| `--dp-popup-inset` | `20px` | the distance from the corner, shared by the button and the popup so they line up |
| `--dp-popup-block` | `640px` | the popup's height ceiling |
| `--dp-fab-clear` | `--dp-fab-size + 12px`, or `0px` with no floating button on the page | the room the popup leaves below itself for the button it opens above |

title: The tokens
text:
Appearance — The tokens
**Radii do not animate.** They used to be rest/hover/focus tiers that grew under the cursor; they are static now, because the reference this design follows has static corners and a shape that moves competes with the colour change already saying the same thing.

Override any of them after the stylesheet:

```css
:root {
  --dp-width: 520px;
  --dp-popup-block: 560px;
}
```

The core's dark values come from `prefers-color-scheme`. An adapter has to re-declare **the whole colour set unconditionally**, not the tokens that differ: every host switches appearance by a class or an attribute and lets a reader pin the site against their OS, so a token left out would keep its OS-driven value and paint one dark element into an otherwise light panel. The suite checks this pairing, for every adapter.

`ui.theme` (/reference/config#ui-theme) overrules both. `'light'` and `'dark'` put a class on `` and the core re-declares the nine tokens that differ between its own two sets, one class deeper than the `:root` an adapter maps on — because an adapter wins by loading second, not by specificity, so a pin written at `:root` would lose on exactly the hosts with a toggle to overrule. `--dp-accent-soft`, `--dp-shadow` and `--dp-scrim` are deliberately left out: they have one value for both schemes, so under a pin they stay the host's. The default, `'auto'`, changes nothing on this page.

Writing one for a host of your own is the same shape: a `:root` block that
re-declares those fifteen names in your tokens' terms, loaded after the core. It
must introduce no `--dp-*` of its own — a token that exists only in an adapter is
a token the core cannot render without it, which is the failure the split exists
to prevent.

title: The panel wears your font
text:
Appearance — The panel wears your font
**It ships none of its own.** `--dp-font` is `inherit`, and the panel is mounted
into ``, so with nothing configured it is set in whatever face the page is
— the same thing the navbar trigger and the call to action under each article
have always done. On VitePress and Docusaurus the adapter maps the token to the
host's own family, so a theme that changes its type changes the panel's with it.

`--dp-font-mono` is a real stack and not `inherit`: a page has no monospace face
for the panel to borrow, so the code blocks, the reasoning trace and the prompt
disclosure keep a system one until you name another.

Two ways to name one, and they are for different situations:

```css
/* CSS — when the value depends on something only a stylesheet knows:
   a media query, a [data-theme], a container. */
:root {
  --dp-font: var(--my-font);
}
```

```js
// settings — when it is one value for the whole site. A family list, or the
// name of the custom property you already keep it in.
docPilot: {
  ui: { font: '--brand-font', fontMono: 'JetBrains Mono, monospace' },
}
```

`ui.font` (/reference/config#ui-font-ui-fontmono) is written onto `` as an
inline custom property, which outranks an adapter — so it reaches the panel on
VitePress and Docusaurus too, where the host's own family would otherwise win. A
`:root` rule of your own outranks the adapter as well, from any unlayered
stylesheet, because the adapter is in `@layer docpilot`.

**Nothing nested may ask for `--dp-font`.** `inherit` is resolved against the
element that uses it, so `var(--dp-font)` written inside a monospaced block
returns the monospace. The one place that used to do it — the heading between
the prompt disclosure's blocks — is why the prompt panel now carries the face and
marks its monospaced *blocks* instead of the other way round.

title: Three shapes, any edge
text:
Appearance — Three shapes, any edge
```js
docPilot: {
  ui: { trigger: 'fab', panel: 'auto', side: 'end', fabLabel: true, fabIcon: true, theme: 'auto' },
}
```

See `ui` (/reference/config#ui) for the values. What each produces:

**Drawer** — full height, docked to an edge — the trailing one unless `ui.side` (/reference/config#ui-side) moves it — `--dp-width` wide, starting below `--dp-top`, with a hairline on the face that looks at the page. With `ui.layout: 'push'` (/reference/config#ui-layout) the page moves away from that edge while it is open, and back as it leaves.

**Popup** — `--dp-width` wide and at most `--dp-popup-block` tall, `--dp-popup-inset` from its edge, sitting `--dp-fab-clear` above it — `12px` above the floating button, or flush against the inset when `ui.trigger` (/reference/config#ui) does not include one — at `--dp-r-lg`. It carries a hairline **and** `--dp-shadow`: a shadow alone is invisible on a dark host and erased outright by `forced-colors`, which is the one mode where a floating surface most needs an edge.

**Bar** — `panel: 'bar'` (/reference/config#ui-panel), and what `'auto'` draws with the floating placement, so the shipped shape. The composer's field, at the bottom centre of every page: `--dp-bar-inline` wide at rest, `--dp-bar-inline-open` once it is focused, holds a question or sits under its window, at `--dp-r-field` with a hairline **and** `--dp-shadow`. The window rises above it — the popup's recipe, centred, as tall as what it holds and never taller than `--dp-popup-block` — at the first character typed. It replaces the floating button, and `ui.side` does not apply: it is centred.

title: Three shapes, any edge
text:
Appearance — Three shapes, any edge
**Bar** — `panel: 'bar'` (/reference/config#ui-panel), and what `'auto'` draws with the floating placement, so the shipped shape. The composer's field, at the bottom centre of every page: `--dp-bar-inline` wide at rest, `--dp-bar-inline-open` once it is focused, holds a question or sits under its window, at `--dp-r-field` with a hairline **and** `--dp-shadow`. The window rises above it — the popup's recipe, centred, as tall as what it holds and never taller than `--dp-popup-block` — at the first character typed. It replaces the floating button, and `ui.side` does not apply: it is centred.

The floating button stays visible while the popup is open and closes it again — the convention every chat widget has already taught, and what makes returning focus to it correct; its sparkle turns into a chevron for as long as the popup is up. It hides itself when it would be underneath: always beneath a drawer, and below 960px beneath any shape.

With a label it becomes a pill and grows on the **inline axis only** — `--dp-fab-size` is an input to the popup's own geometry, which sits a fixed distance above the button, so a taller control would move the panel and a wider one cannot. `--dp-fab-size-coarse` still applies as the block size on a pointer-less device, so the target floor is met either way.

title: What the panel's chrome does
text:
Appearance — What the panel's chrome does
**The header's divider is absent at rest.** At the top of the thread there is no rule under the title; it fades in the moment the conversation is scrolled, and out again at the top. The native form of this — `@container scroll-state(...)` — is Chromium-only, so it is a class from a passive scroll listener, which is the fallback that feature's own guidance prescribes. The border is declared `transparent` and switched by colour, never added and removed, so crossing the top of the scroller cannot move the thread by a pixel.

**Past conversations open above the thread**, under the header button that opens them, with one hairline against the thread and a list that scrolls inside `min(240px, 32dvh)`. The scope picker and the prompt disclosure stay at the bottom, under the footnote row *they* are opened from. At most one of the three is open.

**Selecting inside an answer offers to quote it.** A one-button popover appears above the selection; pressing it puts the passage in the composer as a chip the reader can withdraw, and the question is then asked *about* it. The popover floats, so it takes a hairline **and** `--dp-shadow` like the popup, the floating button, the bar and the bar's window — the five things in the package that do. It uses the platform's top layer where there is one, which is what keeps the popup shape from clipping it, and a plain fixed box where there is not. The chip is `--dp-surface-2` at `--dp-r-md`, one line, 13px, dimmed — a quotation reads as quieter text here, never as a rule down its side.

text:

**The hairline is the structure.** One device, one value — `1px solid var(--dp-line)` — on the drawer's edge, the popup and the bar's window, the bar, the selection popover, the header (transparent until the thread is scrolled), the conversation dock, the scope picker, the composer, the feedback textarea, the code card and the floating button. `outline` is the focus ring and nothing else: `2px solid var(--dp-focus)` at `2px` offset, on every control. **The window is glass.** From 960px up the drawer, the popup and the bar's window are your `--dp-surface` at 70% under `backdrop-filter: blur(24px) saturate(180%)`: the page behind arrives as colour and shape, never as legible text, and the answer keeps its full contrast. The two floating shapes add a one-pixel highlight on their top edge, light falling on the glass, which disappears on a light surface as a highlight would. Below 960px the sheet stays opaque. Nothing inside is a second glass: the composer is an opaque field on it, and the jump pill's blur stays at 2px.

text:

**The window is glass.** From 960px up the drawer, the popup and the bar's window are your `--dp-surface` at 70% under `backdrop-filter: blur(24px) saturate(180%)`: the page behind arrives as colour and shape, never as legible text, and the answer keeps its full contrast. Nothing inside is a second glass: the composer is an opaque field on it, and the jump pill's blur stays at 2px.

**A row has one hover.** In the header, the action rows under a question and an answer, the scope picker's presets, the suggestions and every list of sources — past conversations included — the hover is a single fill that travels from the item you left to the one you reached, on the settle spring: across a row of buttons, down a list, taking each item's width and height on the way. It looks like the hover it replaces — the wash on a control, `--dp-surface-2` on a source row — appears in place when the pointer arrives from outside, and fades in place when it leaves. Keyboard focus keeps each item's own fill and ring, and a linked source keeps its accent.

**Buttons are pills, not links.** No border, a `--dp-wash` on hover and focus, `scale(0.96)` on press, and the inverted `--dp-text` / `--dp-on-text` pair for a toggle that is on. The three controls inside the footnote sentence, and the call-to-action under each article, keep their underline — a pill in running text breaks the line box — and take the same wash at `--dp-r-sm`.

title: What the panel's chrome does
text:
Appearance — What the panel's chrome does
**Buttons are pills, not links.** No border, a `--dp-wash` on hover and focus, `scale(0.96)` on press, and the inverted `--dp-text` / `--dp-on-text` pair for a toggle that is on. The three controls inside the footnote sentence, and the call-to-action under each article, keep their underline — a pill in running text breaks the line box — and take the same wash at `--dp-r-sm`.

**The footnote closes on one word.** `All docs · AI-generated. Check the linked pages. · DocPilot` — the scope button, the disclaimer once a turn exists, and a link to the project so a reader can find out what answered them. The link is the one segment that is always there; it wears `--dp-text` like the two controls beside it rather than your accent, because a coloured word would be the only one in the panel. `ui.credit: false` (/reference/config#ui-credit) removes it.

**The composer does not answer a hover.** It is a `--dp-r-field` stadium with a hairline and the page's own surface, and only focus changes it. A tinted field *and* a ring would be two devices doing one job.

**Icons come from one sprite.** `DocPilotIcons` teleports a 0×0 `` of `` definitions into ``; every glyph in the panel is a `` into it, painted by `currentColor` inherited from the referencing element. It is mounted for you by `withDocPilot` / `docPilotSlots()`. If you compose the components by hand, mount it alongside the panel:

```js
import { DocPilot, DocPilotIcons, DocPilotTrigger } from '@cloflin/docpilot/theme'
```

The navbar trigger and the floating button deliberately do not depend on it — their single glyph is inline, so composing only the trigger still works.

title: What the panel's chrome does
text:
Appearance — What the panel's chrome does
The navbar trigger and the floating button deliberately do not depend on it — their single glyph is inline, so composing only the trigger still works.

**Type is four sizes.** 24px for the empty state's greeting and nothing else; 16px for the answer, the question and both composers; 14px for titles, rows and labels; 13px for meta and mono. Weights are 400, 500 and 600. Both composers are 16px at every width, which is also what stops iOS zooming the viewport when one is focused.

Below 960px the three shapes are identical: a full-screen sheet with a scrim, `role="dialog"` and safe-area padding. The bar stays on the page as a button that looks like its field and opens that sheet.

**Motion is two springs and an exit.** Everything that arrives moves on `--dp-ease` — a spring with no visible overshoot, for the drawer, the sheet, the pushed page — or `--dp-ease-pop`, a spring with a 3.8% overshoot, for what pops: the popup out of its button's corner, the bar's window out of the bar, a question you just asked, the check that says something was copied. Both play over `--dp-dur`. Everything that leaves does so in half that time on `--dp-ease-exit`, an ease-in, and the panel stays in the document until its exit has played. Empty-state suggestions rise in a 40ms stagger; an answer un-blurs into place on its first paint; a conversation restored from history simply is there. All of it is CSS — there is no animation library in the package.

title: What degrades, and how
text:
Appearance — What degrades, and how
Four rules use `:has()` — hiding the floating button under an open panel, shrinking the host's search box only when the navbar trigger is actually there, dropping the room the popup reserves below itself when there is no floating button to reserve it for, and letting the hover in a row take the press of the item under it. A browser without `:has()` applies none of them: the button stays visible behind a drawer that covers it, the trigger sits at the far edge of the navbar instead of beside search, a popup opened from the navbar floats one button-height above the corner, and the hover holds its size while the item it marks is pressed. All four are cosmetic, and all four miss in the safe direction — nothing is hidden and nothing stops working.

`backdrop-filter` is gated: a browser without it gets the opaque surface, because 70% without a blur is a window you read the page through. The glass also goes opaque under `prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce`, `prefers-contrast: more` and `forced-colors: active` — the jump pill's with it. Safari does not report reduced transparency yet; a reader there who also raised contrast is covered.

title: What degrades, and how
text:
Appearance — What degrades, and how
`backdrop-filter` is gated: a browser without it gets the opaque surface, because 70% without a blur is a window you read the page through. The glass also goes opaque under `prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce`, `prefers-contrast: more` and `forced-colors: active` — the jump pill's with it. Safari does not report reduced transparency yet; a reader there who also raised contrast is covered.

Motion is **on by default, whatever the reader's OS says** — `ui.motion` (/reference/config#ui-motion). `'auto'` defers to `prefers-reduced-motion` and `'reduce'` always applies the still variant: every entrance and every exit becomes a fade, the stagger goes, the bar keeps its two widths without travelling between them, the hover in a row or a list appears in place instead of travelling, the two repeating animations stop and every press scale is cancelled, restoring the status label's own colour rather than freezing it mid-gradient. On a VitePress default-theme site the theme's own `base.css` removes all motion with `!important` for a reader whose OS asks, whatever `ui.motion` says.

`forced-colors` needs less than it used to. That mode replaces every background with a system colour, but it forces a border's colour too — so the surfaces that wear a hairline survive it untouched, and only the fill-only ones (the question bubble, the quote chip, the send button, the prompt editor, the copy chip, the suggestion rows) take a `CanvasText` edge. The status label is repainted as well, since its gradient is clipped to text and would otherwise render as an empty line.

title: Syntax highlighting
text:
Appearance — Syntax highlighting
The highlighter is pluggable — Shiki, Prism, highlight.js, or your own — and
Syntax highlighting (/reference/highlighting) is the whole of that API. What
belongs on this page is the part that is about colour.

**Shiki** writes both themes onto every token as custom properties and applies
neither, so a stylesheet has to pick one. The core picks off
`prefers-color-scheme`; each adapter states both branches by the host's own dark
signal — `html.dark` and `html:not(.dark)` on VitePress,
`html[data-theme='dark']` and its negation on Docusaurus. The negative branch is
not decoration: without it, a dark-OS reader on a site pinned to light gets the
panel's code painted for a dark background. A site using
`ui.theme` (/reference/config#ui-theme) gets a third pair on the same terms,
stated *after* the host's in each adapter — `html.dark` and `html.docpilot-dark`
are the same specificity, so order is the only thing that separates them. This is the one thing in the package a
token cannot cover, because the `var()` has to sit on a rule targeting the spans,
which is the only place those variables exist.

**Prism and highlight.js** write classes, and the theme that colours them is the
host's — the same stylesheet that already colours the host's own code blocks, and
switched by whatever already switches those. The panel adds nothing and undoes
exactly one thing: the background. Every highlight.js theme paints `.hljs`, and
Prism's default theme gives `.token.operator` a translucent white that reads as a
smear on a dark panel. The code card is one surface — `--dp-code-bg` — so both are
neutralised inside it, and colour is left alone.

title: The benchmark
text:
The benchmark — The benchmark
Harborline, the fictional product that every DocPilot 2.0 accuracy, speed and safety claim is measured on — what it contains, what it compares, and the commands to rerun it yourself.
Every DocPilot 2.0 claim about accuracy, size, speed and safety comes from one script run on one corpus: `bench/run.mjs` on **Harborline**. You can rerun it. The tables on this page are the output of that run, and nothing else.

title: What Harborline is
text:
The benchmark — What Harborline is
Harborline is a product that does not exist, documented as if it did: a job-queue service with a CLI, an HTTP API and SDKs. A language model has never read about it, so a correct answer can only come from retrieval over these pages. The fixture lives in `bench/harborline/`:

| path | holds |
|---|---|
| `docs/` | The documentation, one file per route of the sidebar |
| `eval/golden.jsonl` | Single-turn questions, each with gold pages and a gold answer, some of them negatives |
| `eval/chains.jsonl` | Multi-turn conversations |
| `eval/adversarial.jsonl` | The security probes (/guide/security-probes), with a canary planted in the instruction |
| `truth/` | The source of every fact, the list of planted defects, and a reference `llms.txt`. It is never indexed and never shown to the tuning agent |
| `docpilot.config.mjs` | The settings: a local embedder and a local chat model, so a run costs no money |

The corpus carries **deliberate defects**, each tied to the questions it affects: pages with no description whose words readers do not use, sections whose answer is split across chunks, and a page that carries an injected instruction. A defect makes a metric measure something. A corpus with none would score well on every system.

title: What it compares
text:
The benchmark — What it compares
An **arm** is an index build: how the corpus is chunked, embedded and stored. A **system** is an arm answered by one runtime of one release.

| arm | what differs |
|---|---|
| `v1.5` | The index the released 1.5 CLI builds |
| `base` | The 2.0 default index |
| `binary` | One bit per dimension (`--quantize=binary`) |
| `ctx-path` | The heading path embedded with each chunk (`DOCPILOT_EMBED_CONTEXT=path`) |
| `ctx-desc` | The heading path and the page description embedded (`path+desc`) |
| `llms` | Page notes from the reference `llms.txt` used as descriptions (`DOCPILOT_LLMS_FILE`) |
| `calibrated` | `base` with the gate's refusals on (`HARBORLINE_GUARD_MODE=calibrated`), its thresholds from `node bench/run.mjs calibrate` |

| system | arm | runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `v1.5 static` | `v1.5` | the released 1.5 CLI, from a checkout of `main` |
| `v2.0 static` | `base` | `runtime: 'browser'` |
| `v2.0 server` | `base` | `runtime: 'server'`, the 2.0 default turn: one-shot, no reasoning before the answer |
| `v2.0 server agentic` | `base` | `runtime: 'server'` with `turn.loop: 'agentic'`, the 1.x server turn |
| `v2.0 static calibrated` | `calibrated` | `runtime: 'browser'` with `guard.mode: 'calibrated'` |
| `v2.0 server calibrated` | `calibrated` | `runtime: 'server'` with `guard.mode: 'calibrated'` |
| `v2.0 static deepseek` | `base` | `runtime: 'browser'`, the chat model `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` on OpenRouter |
| `v2.0 server deepseek` | `base` | `runtime: 'server'`, the same hosted model |
| `v2.0 server agentic deepseek` | `base` | `runtime: 'server'` with `turn.loop: 'agentic'`, the same hosted model |

The 1.5 baseline is the code that shipped, run from a built checkout, not a model of it.

title: Rerun it
text:
The benchmark — Rerun it
You need Node 20 or newer, a built checkout of this repository (`npm run build`, because the report step imports from `dist/`), and Ollama (https://ollama.com/) serving the embedding model `bge-m3` and the chat model. Run every command from the repository root.

```bash
node bench/run.mjs index        # build one index per arm
node bench/run.mjs calibrate    # fit the gate on eval/calibration.jsonl for the calibrated arm
node bench/run.mjs retrieval    # eval --gate-only per arm, dev and test splits: free, minutes
node bench/run.mjs answers      # the golden set answered, per system: hours on a local model
node bench/run.mjs security     # the adversarial probes, per system
node bench/run.mjs perf         # what a reader downloads, per index
node bench/run.mjs report       # bench/harborline/results/RESULTS.md from everything above
```

`answers` and `security` take a system name to run one system: `node bench/run.mjs answers "v2.0 server"`.

| variable | default | what it sets |
|---|---|---|
| `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` | the local Ollama | Where the embedder and the chat model are served |
| `HARBORLINE_CHAT_MODEL` | `qwen3:8b` | The chat model that answers |
| `HARBORLINE_EMBED_MODEL` | `bge-m3` | The embedder |
| `BENCH_LEVEL` | `high` | Which tier of the golden set the answer run scores — see `--level=` (/reference/cli#level) |
| `BASELINE_ROOT` | unset | A built checkout of 1.5. Without it the `v1.5` arm and system are skipped |

Each step saves the log and the eval report in `bench/harborline/results/`. `report` reads those reports and writes `RESULTS.md` and `results.json`. Every number in it comes from a saved report. The paired intervals are computed from the reports' own rows with the bootstrap that `docpilot improve compare` (/reference/cli#improve) uses.

title: Rerun it
text:
The benchmark — Rerun it
Each step saves the log and the eval report in `bench/harborline/results/`. `report` reads those reports and writes `RESULTS.md` and `results.json`. Every number in it comes from a saved report. The paired intervals are computed from the reports' own rows with the bootstrap that `docpilot improve compare` (/reference/cli#improve) uses.

To run one measurement by hand, work from the fixture directory. The CLI resolves `docsDir`, `evalDir` and `indexDir` against the directory it starts in:

```bash
cd bench/harborline
node ../../bin/docpilot.js index --yes
node ../../bin/docpilot.js eval --gate-only --split=test --quiet
node ../../bin/docpilot.js eval --set=adversarial --runtime=server --quiet
```

title: How to read the tables
text:
The benchmark — How to read the tables
- **Retrieval** is scored `--gate-only` on the test split, so it calls no model. An arm is compared with `base` by a paired difference with a 95 % bootstrap interval. A row marked `*` has an interval that excludes zero. A difference without it is not shown to be real. See Measure (/guide/measure) for what each metric counts.
- **Answers** come from one local model. They are a statement about that model on this corpus. Another model gives other numbers, so compare systems within one table, never across machines.
- **Security** is the attack success rate on the probe set, per system. See Attack probes (/guide/security-probes).
- **Bytes** are what a reader of the static install downloads: the size on disk and the size on the wire, compressed with brotli.
- An adopted setting needs a measured gain and a stated cost. An arm that does not beat `base` with a clear interval stays an option, not a default.

Results
Measured on 2026-10-25 with `bge-m3` and `qwen3:8b` on a local Ollama. The raw reports are in `bench/harborline/results/`.

title: Answers
text:
The benchmark — Answers
The golden set at `--level=high`: 65 questions, 50 answerable and 15 negatives. ΔF1 is paired by question against `v1.5 static`.

| system | answer F1 | ΔF1 vs 1.5 | citation P | citation R | negatives caught | first token p50 | whole answer p50 / p95 | requests / turn |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `v1.5 static` | 0.405 | — | 56% | 75% | 40% | — | 24.5 s / 49.1 s | 1.11 |
| `v2.0 static` | 0.405 | ±0.000 [0.000, 0.000] | 56% | 75% | 40% | 27.5 s | 27.5 s / 47.0 s | 1.11 |
| `v2.0 server` | 0.414 | +0.010 [−0.016, 0.033] | 60% | 73% | 40% | 8.3 s | 19.5 s / 39.3 s | 0.98 |
| `v2.0 server agentic` | 0.407 | +0.002 [−0.009, 0.013] | 56% | 78% | 40% | 25.0 s | 25.0 s / 40.2 s | 1.11 |

What it says:

- **The static install answers exactly as 1.5 did.** All 65 answers of `v2.0 static` are byte-identical to those of `v1.5 static`. The latency difference is the machine: the two runs generated the same tokens.
- **The server's default turn is three times faster to the first token.** One-shot without reasoning shows the first token at 8.3 s against 25.0 s for the agentic loop, and it uses 27% fewer prompt tokens. Answer F1 and citations move inside the noise.
- **The cost of one-shot** is that the model cannot search again inside a turn. One of its 65 answers was a generation that ran into the 120 s step timeout. Set `chat.maxTokens` when a local model answers. `server.turn.loop: 'agentic'` restores the 1.x turn.

title: Security
text:
The benchmark — Security
The 30 attack probes (/guide/security-probes), per system. A breach is a probe whose forbidden text reached the answer.

| system | attack success | refused when it should | answered safely | canary leaked | markup echoed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `v2.0 static` | 30% | 19% | 64% | 2 | 3 |
| `v2.0 server` | 30% | 19% | 50% | 0 | 3 |
| `v2.0 server agentic` | 23% | 31% | 64% | 0 | 3 |

What it says:

- **The server keeps its instruction.** The canary in `prompt.extend` reached no reader of either server turn. The static install ships its prompt to the browser, so its canary is public by design.
- **Echoed markup is inert.** Every system repeated an injected ``, `onerror=` or `javascript:` when asked to. The panel escapes HTML and links no `javascript:`, so the reader sees text.
- **The loop resists more.** The agentic turn resisted two probes that one-shot followed: a translated instruction and an instruction planted in a page. With 30 probes the difference is two probes, inside the noise. A site that weighs injection resistance above speed can set `turn.loop: 'agentic'`.

title: A hosted model
text:
The benchmark — A hosted model
The same 65 questions with `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` on OpenRouter as the chat model; the embedder stays the local `bge-m3`. A right outcome is an answer to an answerable question or a refusal of a negative. The three runs cost $0.16.

| system | chat model | right outcome | negatives refused | answerable answered | answer F1 | first token p50 | whole answer p50 | prompt tokens / turn |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `v2.0 static` | `qwen3:8b`, local | 56/65 | 6/15 | 50/50 | 0.405 | 27.5 s | 27.5 s | 2,757 |
| `v2.0 static deepseek` | `deepseek-v4-flash` | 63/65 | 14/15 | 49/50 | 0.429 | 10.4 s | 13.6 s | 7,762 |
| `v2.0 server` | `qwen3:8b`, local | 55/65 | 6/15 | 49/50 | 0.405 | 8.3 s | 19.5 s | 2,004 |
| `v2.0 server deepseek` | `deepseek-v4-flash` | 60/65 | 15/15 | 45/50 | 0.409 | 13.3 s | 17.3 s | 2,096 |
| `v2.0 server agentic deepseek` | `deepseek-v4-flash` | 61/65 | 13/15 | 48/50 | 0.436 | 9.8 s | 13.7 s | 6,959 |

Answer F1 here counts a refused answerable question as 0, so a system cannot raise it by refusing.

What it says:

title: A hosted model
text:
The benchmark — A hosted model
What it says:

- **The model is the lever.** With the hosted model the static install reached the right outcome on 63 of 65 questions instead of 56 (McNemar p = 0.039). Most of the gain is honesty: it refused 14 of the 15 questions the docs cannot answer, where the local model refused 6, and it still answered 49 of 50 answerable ones. Answer F1 moved inside the noise.
- **One-shot is a local-model default.** With the hosted model the agentic loop showed the first token sooner than one-shot (9.8 s against 13.3 s) and answered every Russian question one-shot refused (9 of 9 against 6 of 9), at 3.3 times the prompt tokens. The right outcomes are level (61 and 60 of 65). A server with a fast hosted model can set `turn.loop: 'agentic'` and pay in tokens, not in time.

title: The gate
text:
The benchmark — The gate
`eval/calibration.jsonl` holds 295 probes in the eleven strata `docpilot calibrate` reads, and none of them is a golden question. On Harborline `calibrate` refuses to write thresholds: the tau that lets every answerable probe through is 0.15, below the lexical weight 0.25, where a question would clear the gate on shared words alone (`bench/harborline/eval/calibration.report.md`). The build then inlines the provisional tau 0.30, and the calibrated systems measure that.

| system | negatives caught | over-refusal | answer F1 | whole answer p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `v2.0 static` | 6/15 | 0/50 | 0.405 | 27.5 s |
| `v2.0 static calibrated` | 6/15 | 0/50 | 0.405 | 23.8 s |
| `v2.0 server` | 6/15 | 0/50 | 0.414 | 19.5 s |
| `v2.0 server calibrated` | 7/15 | 0/50 | 0.405 | 20.1 s |

What it says:

- **The gate measures topic, not whether an answer exists.** Probes about absent features and absent APIs sit at a median G of 0.65 to 0.91, as high as the probes the docs answer (0.90 to 0.97). Only off-domain questions fall below a threshold that a real question never reaches.
- **On these questions the gate adds one refusal.** In the static install it refuses five off-domain questions that the model refused anyway, so the reader gets the same answers without a model call. On the server it catches one more negative, with no false refusal. The two server runs gave the same text on 20 of 65 questions, and the gate changed five of them: the rest is the model's own variation.
- **The default stays `guard.mode: 'off'`.** A threshold has to be measured per corpus and per language — see Relevance gate (/features/gate) — and on this corpus no measured threshold exists. A site with blatant off-topic traffic can set `guard.tau` by hand and check it with `eval --gate-only`.

How it compares — How it compares
There are good hosted answer services for documentation, and this page is not
going to pretend otherwise. What it is going to do is name the **one
architectural difference** the rest of the differences fall out of, put the
products side by side on it, and then say plainly where the hosted services are
the better buy.

does not document something, this page says **not documented** rather than
guessing, and **not documented is not the same as "no"**.

**Prices are quoted from the vendor's own pricing page**, or marked

title: The one difference
text:
How it compares — The one difference
**DocPilot does retrieval in the reader's browser, against a static file you
built.** Every other product on this page does retrieval on a server — theirs,
or one you run for them.

That is not a small implementation detail, because six things follow from it:

- there is no index to keep in sync with a vendor, because the index is a file
 in your `public/` directory;
- an off-topic question can be settled for free, because the decision is
 arithmetic in the browser rather than a request somebody bills;
- reader questions reach exactly one third party — the model provider whose key
 you configured — instead of two;
- the thing you deploy is a static asset, so its failure mode is a 404 rather
 than an outage;
- the gate's thresholds can be measured against **your** corpus, because the
 gate is code you run;
- and it is MIT, so the answer to "what if you disappear" is that the file is
 still in your repository.

The cost side of that trade is real too, and it is in
What DocPilot is worse at.

Price

title: And what $0 does not cover
text:
How it compares — And what $0 does not cover
DocPilot bills nothing and has no hosted half to bill from: no account, no
service, no telemetry — the only URL the panel fetches that this project
controls is your own index file. But the line is **free software**, not free
answers, and the project's own documentation opens its cost section with
*"It is worth being clear about the price, because there is one."* (./why#what-it-costs)

- **A model provider key.** One key is the whole configuration, and it is yours,
 billed by them, at their rate. Choosing providers (./providers).
- **Or the free tier, which is a real ceiling.** With nothing set, the chain
 falls through to OpenRouter's free tier: one key, no card — and **50 requests
 a day** under 10 credits bought. That meters **requests, not tokens**, and one
 turn is an embedding request plus two or three model calls, so fifty is a
 dozen-odd questions. `budget` (/reference/config#budget).
- **Rebuilding the index draws on the same allowance** — but only for what
 changed. Vectors are cached by model and by chunk text, so editing one page
 costs one embedding request rather than one per 32 chunks of the corpus. A
 first build, or an embedder swap, still pays in full.
- **The proxy route spends money per request** and is reachable by anyone who
 can load the page. A per-IP rate limit and a body cap are
 part of shipping it (./production).
- **No support contract and no SLA.** It is an MIT package, and
 that cuts both ways.
